Chapter 4 · Origins · c. 400–1450

Transmission and transformation of knowledge in the Middle Ages

Augustine, Avicenna, Alhazen, the hospitals of Baghdad and Cairo and the Valencia hospital of 1409: the Middle Ages preserved, debated and extended knowledge about the mind.

The Middle Ages are often presented as a dark interlude between Antiquity and the Renaissance. For the history of the mind they were rather a time of translation and new ideas, above all in the Islamic world, from Baghdad to Córdoba.

What were people trying to understand?

How soul and body relate, how perception, imagination and memory work, and how to care for people suffering from mental disorders. In the Christian world, inner life was also explored: will, guilt and self-knowledge.

With what methods?

Translation of and commentary on Greek texts, clinical observation in hospitals and, in at least one remarkable case, experiment. Augustine of Hippo (354–430) wrote pages on memory in the Confessions that are still astonishing: he describes it as a "vast palace" in which we store images, past emotions and even the memory of having forgotten. His method was to look inwards, an early form of introspection.

Who took part?

In Baghdad, the House of Wisdom translated Aristotle and Galen into Arabic. The Persian physician Al-Razi (c. 865–925) ran hospitals and wrote on melancholy and its treatment. Avicenna (980–1037) systematised, in the Canon of Medicine and his philosophical works, the theory of the internal senses: common sense, imagination, estimation, memory. He placed them in different parts of the brain, an early form of localising functions. Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham, c. 965–1040) showed in his Book of Optics that we see because light reaches the eyes, not because the eyes emit rays, and studied visual illusions and the role of judgement in perception, often through experiments. In Europe, Thomas Aquinas integrated Aristotle into Christian theology.

Hospitals in the Islamic world, called bimaristans, often included sections for the mentally ill, with music, baths and conversation as part of their care. In 1409 the friar Gilabert Jofré promoted the Hospital of the Innocents in Valencia, considered one of the first hospitals in Europe specifically devoted to people with mental disorders.

What did it contribute?

  • The preservation and critique of the Greek legacy, which reached Europe largely through Arabic.
  • A theory of perception based on experiment, Alhazen's.
  • The first schemes of mental functions located in the brain.
  • Institutions devoted to the care of people with mental illness.

What was revised later?

Placing the internal senses in the brain's ventricles, an idea that lasted until the Renaissance, was wrong: functions depend on tissue, not on fluid-filled cavities. And the coexistence of medicine with religious explanations was complex; not all of the Middle Ages treated madness as possession, but not all of it treated madness as illness either. The image of a "dark" age has been heavily revised, and the role of translations and of scholars from al-Andalus, such as Averroes and Maimonides, in passing on knowledge is now widely recognised.
